disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c is in the diabetes range, and together with a BMI in the obese range, low activity, current smoking, and several existing health conditions, this adds extra strain on your heart, kidneys, liver and blood vessels. The most valuable next steps are getting your lipid profile, kidney function, liver check, blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessed soon since these are highlighted priorities, building in regular gentle physical activity, and following the food guidance on sodium, saturated fat and calories. Small, steady changes can meaningfully support your health over time.

risk_factors.label: Existing health condition: High blood pressure
Existing health condition: High cholesterol or triglycerides
Existing health condition: Heart or blood-vessel disease
Existing health condition: Fatty liver disease

comorbidity_assessment.note: High blood pressure and elevated blood glucose often occur together and both strain blood vessels, so controlling sodium intake and staying active can help both.
Abnormal cholesterol levels raise cardiovascular risk alongside elevated glucose, making regular lipid checks and lower saturated fat intake especially important.
Extra body weight increases insulin resistance, which can raise blood glucose, so gradual weight loss is one of the most helpful steps you can take.
Elevated blood glucose can add to strain already placed on the heart and blood vessels, so cardiovascular monitoring and safe activity levels matter.
High blood glucose can affect kidney filtering over time, so keeping an eye on kidney function and following protein and sodium guidance is important.
Thyroid hormones influence metabolism and energy, and an imbalance can make weight and blood glucose management more challenging.
Fat buildup in the liver is linked with insulin resistance, so weight loss and reduced saturated fat can support both liver and blood glucose health.
Poor sleep quality from sleep apnoea can affect blood glucose control, and weight loss may help ease both conditions.

constraints: Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day (about one teaspoon of salt in total); avoid pickles, papad, instant noodles and salty snacks.
Follow a DASH-style pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses and low-fat dairy (or fortified alternatives).
Keep saturated fat low (limit ghee, butter, coconut oil, red and processed meat); avoid trans fats (vanaspati, many fried and bakery foods).
Include soluble fibre daily (oats, barley, pulses, psyllium) and unsaturated fats (nuts, seeds, olive or mustard oil in small amounts).
Follow the calorie target; avoid sugary drinks and fruit juices completely.
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables to stay full on fewer calories.
Keep sodium under 2,300 mg a day and saturated fat low.
Prefer fish, pulses and nuts over red and processed meat (plant proteins for vegetarian and vegan users).
Do not follow high-protein diets or take protein supplements; keep protein moderate unless your kidney doctor advises otherwise.
Do not use potassium-based salt substitutes; ask your doctor whether you need to limit potassium or phosphorus.
Do not take iodine or kelp supplements unless prescribed.
Cut added sugars and sugary drinks, especially fructose-sweetened ones.
Avoid alcohol and heavy meals within 3 hours of bedtime.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables like spinach, bottle gourd, capsicum and cauliflower
Whole grains and millets such as brown rice, bajra and jowar
Pulses and legumes like moong dal, chana and rajma
Oats and barley for soluble fibre
Fish and skinless chicken in small portions instead of red or processed meat
Unsalted nuts and seeds in small amounts
Low-fat dairy like buttermilk or curd in moderation
Fresh whole fruits such as guava, apple and papaya in limited portions
foods_to_avoid: Instant noodles and packaged processed foods
Deep-fried foods and bakery items made with vanaspati or trans fats
Ghee, butter and coconut oil in large amounts
Potassium-based salt substitutes unless advised by a doctor
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with whole grains like brown rice or millets, and one quarter with a pulse or small portion of fish or chicken. Keep oil use to one to two teaspoons per meal and avoid adding extra salt at the table.
plan.hydration: Drink about 8 to 10 glasses of plain water through the day. Avoid sugary drinks, packaged juices and alcohol completely. Herbal teas without sugar are a good option.
based_on: high blood pressure: DASH-style, low sodium
high cholesterol: low saturated fat, unsaturated fats preferred
kidney disease: moderate protein, no potassium substitutes
heart disease: limit saturated fat and sodium
sleep apnoea: avoid heavy meals near bedtime

exercise: Because you have heart or blood-vessel disease, please get medical clearance from your doctor before starting any new or vigorous exercise programme.
Start gently with short sessions of low-impact activity, such as 5-10 minutes of slow walking or seated exercises, to protect your joints.
Gradually build up toward 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking or swimming, as your fitness and clearance allow.
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities (like light resistance bands or bodyweight moves) on 2 days a week once cleared.
Adjust your pace and goals based on your energy levels, since thyroid issues can affect how you feel day to day.
Stop exercise immediately and seek medical help if you feel chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 10 minutes of gentle walking once a day, 4 days a week. Slowly build up to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as your doctor confirms it's safe and your fitness improves.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range. A gradual weight loss of about 5-10% of your current body weight over 6 months can help improve blood pressure, cholesterol, liver fat and sleep apnoea severity. Focus on small, steady changes to meals and activity rather than quick fixes. This is not about dieting hard but building sustainable habits over time.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a regular bedtime and wake time, even on weekends. Use your prescribed breathing device every night if you have one for sleep apnoea, as this can help improve sleep quality and support weight and blood pressure goals. Avoid screens and caffeine close to bedtime, and keep your bedroom cool and dark.
stress: Try slow breathing exercises for 5-10 minutes a day, breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6, to help calm your nervous system.
Consider gentle mindfulness or meditation practices, even just 5 minutes a day, to help manage daily stress.
Light activities like gentle yoga or stretching (once cleared by your doctor) can also help release tension.
behaviour_change: Since you currently smoke, consider reaching out to a quitline or your doctor for support in quitting. Stopping smoking can significantly help your heart, kidney and liver health.
Try setting one small, specific goal each week, like adding a 10-minute walk or swapping one snack for a healthier option, rather than trying to change everything at once.
Avoid regular use of painkillers such as ibuprofen without checking with your doctor first, especially given your kidney health.
Track your progress in a simple journal or app to notice patterns and celebrate small wins.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Vitamin D
monitoring.why: Low vitamin D is more common with obesity and kidney disease; testing is not routine for everyone.
monitoring.frequency: Only if your doctor recommends it

monitoring.name: Thyroid function (TSH)
monitoring.why: Thyroid problems affect weight, energy and blood glucose control.
monitoring.frequency: Every 6–12 months, or as your doctor advises

preventive_actions: Schedule lipid profile, kidney function, liver check, dilated eye exam, foot exam, blood pressure and cardiovascular risk assessment as soon as you can, since these are flagged as priorities.
Aim for gentle, regular aerobic activity, building up slowly and getting medical clearance first given your heart condition.
Follow the sodium limit of under 2,300 mg a day and reduce saturated fat by cutting back on ghee, butter and processed meats.
Work toward the 1,300 calorie target with vegetables filling half your plate, and avoid sugary drinks and alcohol completely.
Consider support to quit smoking, as it adds extra risk to your heart and blood vessels.
Keep a consistent sleep routine and use any prescribed breathing support every night to help with sleep apnoea.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
